title: Troubleshooting Applications
summary: Pod states, describe and events, logs, exec, kubectl debug and termination messages: symptom to command.

blocks.text: Start every app investigation with `kubectl describe`. It shows container state, restarts and recent events. Then follow the branch that matches what you see.
kubectl describe pods <pod-name>

header: What it means / what to check
rows: Can't be scheduled. Read the scheduler messages in describe: not enough CPU/memory, or a `hostPort` limiting where it fits
Scheduled but can't start. Most often an image pull failure: check the image name, that it was pushed, and try pulling it by hand
Deletion requested but not finished. Usually a finalizer plus a webhook (`ValidatingWebhookConfiguration` / `MutatingWebhookConfiguration`) that blocks UPDATE on pods
A key in the spec may be misspelled or mis-nested and silently ignored

blocks.text: For the last case, recreate the Pod with validation on, and diff what the API server stored against your file:

kubectl apply --validate -f <file>.yaml
kubectl get pods/<pod-name> -o yaml > <pod-name>-on-apiserver.yaml
Pending fixes from the page: delete Pods, lower resource requests, or add nodes. If you need `hostPort`, you can run at most one such Pod per node.

items: A container's **State** is `Waiting`, `Running` or `Terminated`, with extra detail for each.
**Ready** reports whether the last readiness probe passed. With no probe, the container counts as ready.
**Restart Count** climbing is your hint of a crash loop (restart policy `Always`).
**Events** list what happened: `From` is the reporting component; `Reason` and `Message` explain it.

blocks.text: A Pod that fits on no node shows a `FailedScheduling` event from the scheduler with the per-node reason (for example, not enough CPU). One fix shown is `kubectl scale` to fewer replicas.

kubectl get events
kubectl get events --namespace=<namespace>
kubectl get pod <pod-name> -o yaml

items: Events are **namespaced**. Pass `--namespace`, or `--all-namespaces` to see everything.
`-o yaml` shows everything the system holds about the Pod, beyond describe.

blocks.text: A crashing container in describe looks like `State: Waiting` with `Reason: CrashLoopBackOff`, and `Last State: Terminated` with the exit code.
Write to **stdout/stderr** and Kubernetes captures it. `kubectl logs` asks the kubelet, which reads the log file on the node.

kubectl logs <pod-name>
kubectl logs <pod-name> -c <container-name>   # multi-container Pods
kubectl logs <pod-name> --previous            # the previous instance (after a crash)

items: On a restart, the kubelet keeps **one** terminated container and its logs. Evicting a Pod removes its containers and their logs.
Log rotation is set in the kubelet config: `containerLogMaxSize` (default **10Mi**) and `containerLogMaxFiles` (default **5**).
`kubectl logs` only returns the **latest** log file, so you may see at most one rotation's worth.
By default the runtime writes container logs under `/var/log/pods` (changeable with the kubelet's `podLogsDir`).
Kubernetes has no built-in log storage. Cluster-level logging needs a separate backend, often fed by a node agent run as a **DaemonSet**.

blocks.text: App writes to files instead? A **streaming sidecar** can tail each file to its own stdout, so `kubectl logs <pod-name> <sidecar-name>` works. A sidecar that runs its own logging agent does **not** show up in `kubectl logs`.

kubectl logs -f <pod-name>                        # stream
kubectl logs -f <pod-name> -c <container-name>
kubectl logs -l <label>=<value>                   # by label
kubectl logs -f -l <label>=<value> --all-containers
kubectl logs deploy/<deployment-name>
kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
kubectl events --types=Warning
kubectl get pods --sort-by='.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount'
`kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp` lists events sorted by timestamp, and `kubectl events --types=Warning` lists only the warnings.
If the image has tools, run them in place. `-c` is optional for single-container Pods.

kubectl exec <pod-name> -c <container-name> -- <cmd> <args>
kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- sh
No shell (distroless) or the container already crashed? Add an **ephemeral container** (stable since v1.25):
kubectl debug -it <pod-name> --image=busybox:1.28 --target=<container-name>

items: `--target` joins the process namespace of that container. The runtime must support it.
The ephemeral container is listed under **Ephemeral Containers** in `kubectl describe pod`.

blocks.text: Or debug a **copy** of the Pod:

# copy + extra container, shared process namespace
kubectl debug <pod-name> -it --image=ubuntu --share-processes --copy-to=<pod-name>-debug
# copy with a container's command replaced by a shell
kubectl debug <pod-name> -it --copy-to=<pod-name>-debug --container=<container-name> -- sh
# copy with every image swapped
kubectl debug <pod-name> --copy-to=<pod-name>-debug --set-image=*=ubuntu

items: To change an existing container's command you must name it with `--container`; otherwise a new container is added.
`--attach=false` stops auto-attach; reconnect with `kubectl attach`.
Profiles via `--profile`: `legacy` (current default, planned for deprecation), `general`, `baseline`, `restricted`, `netadmin`, `sysadmin`.
Clean up afterwards: `kubectl delete pod <pod-name> <pod-name>-debug`.

sections.heading: Termination messages
sections.sourceTitle: Determine the Reason for Pod Failure

blocks.text: A container can write a short final status to a file. Kubernetes copies it into the container's status so tools can show it.

items: Default file: `terminationMessagePath` = `/dev/termination-log`. It can't be changed after the Pod starts.
The kubelet truncates a message over **4096 bytes**. All containers share **12KiB** in total, split equally.

`terminationMessagePolicy`: `File` (default) or `FallbackToLogsOnError`, which uses the end of the log when the file is empty and the container failed (max **2048 bytes or 80 lines**, whichever is smaller).

blocks.text: kubectl get pod <pod-name> -o go-template="{{range .status.containerStatuses}}{{.lastState.terminated.message}}{{end}}"
In `-o yaml`, look under `status.containerStatuses[].lastState.terminated.message`, next to `exitCode`.

flashcards.front: First command for any misbehaving Pod?
flashcards.back: `kubectl describe pods <pod-name>`: container state, restarts and recent events.

flashcards.front: A Pod stays Pending. What does that mean?
flashcards.back: It can't be scheduled. Check scheduler messages: insufficient CPU/memory, or `hostPort` restrictions.

flashcards.front: A Pod stays Waiting. Most common cause?
flashcards.back: Failing to pull the image. Check the name, that it was pushed, and try a manual pull.

flashcards.front: A Pod is stuck Terminating. What should you suspect?
flashcards.back: A finalizer plus an admission webhook that blocks UPDATE operations on pods.

flashcards.front: How do you catch a misspelled field such as `commnd`?
Get logs from the crashed previous instance of a container?
Kubelet log rotation settings and defaults?
Default directory for container logs on a Linux node?
Container image has no shell. How do you get a shell in that Pod?

flashcards.back: Creates a copy of the Pod with changes (extra container, new command, new images), leaving the original alone.
If the message file is empty and the container errored, use the tail of the log (max 2048 bytes or 80 lines).

questions.stem: A Pod has been in Pending for ten minutes. What does Pending most directly tell you?

options.text: It can't be scheduled onto a node
options.explanation: Pending means the scheduler hasn't placed it; describe shows why.
Image pull problems show up after scheduling, as a Waiting container.

options.text: The container exited with an error
options.explanation: That would show a Terminated/crashing container, not an unscheduled Pod.
That's the Terminating case.

questions.stem: `kubectl describe pod` shows a container in `Waiting` on a node. According to the debug guide, what is the most common cause?

options.explanation: The guide calls image pull failure the most common cause of Waiting.

options.text: The node has no CPU left
options.explanation: Lack of resources keeps the Pod Pending (unscheduled), not Waiting on a node.
Services don't stop a container from starting.

options.text: The termination message is too long
options.explanation: That only truncates a message.

questions.stem: Your app container crashed and restarted. Which command shows the output from the crashed instance?

options.explanation: `--previous` reads the earlier instance's log.
`-f` streams the current instance.
Events show what happened, not app output.
Shows resource usage, not output.

questions.stem: True or false: `kubectl get events` with no flags shows events from every namespace.

options.explanation: Events are namespaced; you need `--all-namespaces`.
Correct. Without a namespace flag you only see the current namespace.

questions.stem: A Pod runs a distroless image with no shell, so `kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh` fails. What's the documented way in?

options.explanation: Adds an ephemeral container with tools, sharing the target's process namespace.
The page uses attach only to reconnect to a debug session; it adds no debugging tools.
Shows logs only; no interactive access.
Shows the full object; doesn't open a shell.

questions.stem: Which commands show container log output? Select 3.

options.explanation: Streams the Pod's logs.
Dumps logs from Pods matching the label.
Dumps logs from a Deployment's Pod.
Lists warning events, not container output.
Shows CPU/memory usage, not logs.

questions.stem: A Pod writes 40 MiB of logs and the kubelet rotates at 10 MiB. How much can `kubectl logs` return?

options.text: At most 10 MiB, only the latest file
options.explanation: Only the latest log file is served.
Older rotated files aren't returned.
The latest file is readable.

options.text: Exactly 5 files' worth, one per containerLogMaxFiles
options.explanation: Only the latest file is returned, whatever the file count setting.

questions.stem: Which are true about kubelet log handling? Select 2.

options.explanation: Stated default.
Stated default.

options.text: Kubernetes ships a native log storage backend
options.explanation: It doesn't; you need a separate backend.

options.text: Evicted Pods keep their container logs on the node
options.explanation: Evicting a Pod also removes its containers' logs.

questions.stem: You run a logging agent inside a sidecar container. Which limitation does the logging page call out?

options.text: Those logs aren't available through kubectl logs
options.explanation: They aren't controlled by the kubelet.

options.text: The sidecar must run as a DaemonSet
options.explanation: DaemonSets are for node-level agents, not sidecars.

options.text: The Pod can't use emptyDir volumes
options.explanation: The example sidecars share an emptyDir.

options.text: The app must stop writing to stdout
options.explanation: No such requirement.

questions.stem: Where does a container write its termination message by default?

options.explanation: The default `terminationMessagePath`.
That's the page's example of a custom `terminationMessagePath`.
The message comes from a file; logs are only a fallback with FallbackToLogsOnError.
Kubernetes reads it from the file and puts it into the container status.

questions.stem: True or false: With `terminationMessagePolicy: FallbackToLogsOnError`, Kubernetes uses the end of the container log if the message file is empty and the container exited with an error.

options.explanation: Correct. The fallback is capped at 2048 bytes or 80 lines, whichever is smaller.
That is exactly what the policy does.

questions.stem: You want to change the command of container `app` in a crashing Pod to `sh`, without touching the original Pod. Which command fits?

options.explanation: Copies the Pod and replaces app's command.
Without `--container`, kubectl debug adds a new container instead.
A crashing container won't stay up for exec, and this doesn't change its command.
That swaps images, not the command.

questions.stem: A Pod spec has `commnd` instead of `command` and the Pod runs the wrong thing. What does the guide suggest first?

options.text: Delete it and recreate with kubectl apply --validate -f <file>.yaml
options.explanation: Validation flags the unknown field.
Logs won't reveal an ignored spec key.
Doesn't fix the spec.
The kubelet ran what the API server stored.

questions.stem: A Pod is stuck in Terminating. Which belong to the documented diagnosis? Select 2.

options.text: Check for a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration or MutatingWebhookConfiguration targeting pod UPDATEs
options.explanation: A webhook can block finalizer removal.

options.text: Look for a finalizer on the Pod
options.explanation: The scenario needs a finalizer the control plane can't remove.

options.text: Check that the image was pushed to the registry
options.explanation: That's for Waiting Pods.
That's for Pending Pods.

questions.explanation: `kubectl logs` prints a container's stdout and stderr.

questions.stem: Show the logs of the previous, crashed instance of the container in Pod `my-pod`.
questions.explanation: After a restart, the current container's logs may be empty; `--previous` shows the last terminated instance.

questions.stem: Show the logs of container `my-container` in the multi-container Pod `my-pod`.
questions.explanation: With more than one container, `-c` (`--container`) picks which container's logs to show.

questions.stem: Open an interactive `/bin/sh` shell in the single-container Pod `my-pod`.
questions.explanation: `--stdin --tty` (short: `-it`) attach your terminal; everything after `--` is the command run in the container.

labs.title: Investigate a crashing Pod
labs.scenario: Pod `my-pod` keeps restarting. Narrow down why.

steps.prompt: List the Pods in the namespace and look at STATUS and RESTARTS.
steps.explanation: A rising RESTARTS count points to a container that keeps exiting.

steps.prompt: Show the details and recent events for `my-pod`.
steps.explanation: `describe` shows container states, exit reasons and the Pod's events.

steps.prompt: Show the logs of the previous, crashed container in `my-pod`.
steps.explanation: The crashed instance's output usually holds the error.

steps.prompt: List the namespace's events, oldest first.
steps.explanation: Sorting by creation time shows what happened in order.
